title: AI for Financial Modeling: What It Does and 5 Tools
summary: AI for financial modeling can draft a DCF or three-statement model in minutes. Here's what it does well, the 5 tools worth using, and how to check its work.
body_markdown:
AI for financial modeling means using AI tools like Shortcut and Claude for Excel to build, populate, and stress-test a model. You describe what you need in a prompt or hand over a document, and you get back formulas already wired.


I've used AI on the same jobs a finance team handles weekly, like pulling historicals from a filing, linking a three-statement model, and flexing a few scenarios.


Here's the honest read on what these tools can do in a model, where they break, and how to check their work before anyone signs off.


## What is AI for financial modeling?


AI for financial modeling **uses AI to build financial models, projections, and budgets** . You describe what you need in a prompt (or hand over a document), and the AI wires the formulas into the model for you. It also shows you where each number came from, so you can click through and check its work.


This is different from AI data analysis. Analysis works with numbers you already have, like last quarter's sales. If that's your job,[other tools fit better](https://julius.ai/articles/best-financial-analysis-tools-for-business-data) .


Modeling is different: **you're working out numbers that don't exist yet, based on what might happen next** . That's a harder job for AI, since some of those numbers depend on each other. Change one number and three others move too. AI can lose track of that chain, and that's often where mistakes creep in.


## What AI does inside a model


Strip away the marketing, **and AI does four jobs in a model:**


- **Pulls numbers out of documents:** Point it at a report, a PDF, or a transcript, and you can get the historical numbers back in a tab. How much cleanup that takes depends on the tool. Some handle this with a straight drag-and-drop, while others need you to reformat the file first.
- **Builds the linked structure:** You get a three-statement model where the three parts talk to each other. Change one number, and the other two update too.
- **Runs different scenarios:** Ask for a good case, a bad case, and one in between, and you get numbers for each version.
- **Drafts the narrative:** You get a first pass at the write-up explaining why the numbers moved. That's usually the part that eats an afternoon.


**💡 Note:** AI saves the most time on pulling numbers and drafting the first pass. You still have to set the assumptions, make the judgment calls, and do the final check.


## The models AI can build: DCF, LBO, three-statement, and forecasting


AI handles some model types better than others. **Here's the honest read on the four you'll build most:**


### Three-statement models


A three-statement model **links three reports together** : the income statement, the balance sheet, and the cash flow statement. Change one number, and the other two should update too.


**AI is decent at building that link, but it struggles with one specific problem** : interest payments. What a company pays in interest depends on how much debt it holds and how much cash it has on hand, and those two numbers can shift as the model runs.


When AI hits that problem, one of two things happens. The model shows an error and stops working, or AI types in a fixed number instead of letting the formula work it out. Either way, **you'll need to check that section yourself** before you trust it.


### DCF models


A DCF, or discounted cash flow model, **estimates what a company is worth today based on the cash it's expected to make** in the future. AI can build the structure for this from a prompt, and that structure usually holds up.


The assumptions behind it are shakier. Growth rate, the discount rate, and the final value at the end of the projection are the numbers AI tends to guess at with a default that sounds reasonable (but may not fit your company). Check those numbers before you trust them.


### LBO models


An LBO, or leveraged buyout model, **shows what happens when a company is bought using mostly borrowed money** . This is the hardest model type for AI. The debt payments, cash use, and investor returns all depend on each other, and AI tends to get the big picture right while missing the details that decide the actual return.


Comps and merger models fall in between DCF and LBO. The more their numbers depend on each other, the more you'll need to double-check.


### Budgeting and forecasting


**This is the strongest fit for AI** , especially for teams building budgets or rolling forecasts. These models are more forgiving than a valuation, since there's less riding on any one number. If you build forecasts in Excel, pairing AI with a[dependable forecasting method](https://julius.ai/articles/how-to-forecast-in-excel) gets you most of the way there.


## 5 AI financial modeling tools worth knowing


Five names show up again and again in this space. **Let’s compare them below:**


**💻 Tool** **🎯 Best for** **⚡ Strengths** **❌ Watch-outs** **🔥 Where it runs**


**Shortcut** Building real models in Excel Built only for modeling, sets up structure fast Costs more, narrow focus, newer to the market Excel-native


**Claude for Excel** Working through logic and catching errors Strong at explaining its work and checking for mistakes Takes setup, still rolling out to everyone Excel add-in


**Microsoft Copilot** Teams already using Microsoft 365 Wide rollout, works right where you already are Builds a simpler model that can hide gaps Excel-native


**ChatGPT** Formula help and explaining logic Now works inside the workbook, cites the cells it changes Newer to Excel, so still catching up on deep model-building Excel add-in


**Excel add-in category** Quick formulas and one-off tasks Fast for small, specific jobs Won't build a full model Excel add-in


- **[Shortcut](https://shortcut.ai/) :** Built only for financial modeling inside Excel, and the one most likely to hand you a usable structure from a prompt. It costs more and has a narrow focus, so it's easiest to justify if modeling is your main job.
- **[Claude for Excel](https://claude.com/excel) :** Strong at walking through model logic and catching errors. That's part of why Corporate Finance Institute built[a full course](https://corporatefinanceinstitute.com/course/ai-financial-modeling-claude-excel-course/) around using it to audit models. Setup takes a minute, and it's still rolling out to everyone.
- **[Microsoft Copilot](https://copilot.microsoft.com/) :** Already sitting inside your Excel if your company runs on Microsoft 365. It can build something that looks like a full model, but watch for hardcoded numbers or scenario switches that aren't actually linked. Give it a check before you trust the output.
- **[ChatGPT](https://chatgpt.com/) :** Fast and cheap for explaining what a model needs,[debugging a formula](https://julius.ai/articles/chatgpt-in-excel) , or drafting logic. With ChatGPT for Excel, it now works inside the workbook too, updating cells and formulas directly and asking before it makes a change, similar to how Claude for Excel and Copilot work.
- **Excel add-in category:** Fast for small, specific jobs like writing one formula or cleaning up a column. Not built to produce a full linked model.


Go with Shortcut or Claude for Excel if you're building inside the workbook, Copilot if you already live in Microsoft 365, and ChatGPT if you mainly need help thinking it through.


## Where AI models break: accuracy and failure modes


Every AI-built model looks finished, but that's the trap. The output looks confident whether the numbers are right or made up, **so you have to know the specific ways it fails:**


- **Hallucinated historicals:** The model fills in past numbers that look right but don't match the actual filing.[Research on LLMs in finance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.15548) has found these models can generate financial facts, like stock prices, that are confidently wrong, which is the same failure mode showing up here.
- **Hardcoded values:** A number gets typed straight into a cell instead of built from a formula. When an input changes later, that cell doesn't update.
- **Broken links:** The three linked reports (income statement, balance sheet, cash flow) fall out of sync, and the balance sheet stops balancing.
- **Stuck loops:** Interest and debt don't work themselves out the way they should. The model either shows an error or fakes a fixed number instead.
- **Weak deal logic:** Mergers, buyouts, and company restructuring are where AI's reasoning is thinnest, and its mistakes cost the most.


None of this is new to spreadsheets.[Research on real-world spreadsheets](https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.02601) found that most large spreadsheets have at least one wrong number hiding somewhere, and that was true long before AI started building them. **AI just makes those errors faster and dresses them up** in clean formatting.


My recommendation: **treat an AI-built model as a fast first draft** . It gets you to a starting point in minutes, but not to something you'd stake a decision on. That's why the next step matters.


## How to audit an AI-built model before you rely on it


Every guide on this topic says "trust but verify" and then leaves you to figure out the verify part. **Here's the checklist I run in Excel on any model an AI hands me:**


1. **Trace the historicals to the source:** Pick a handful of past-year numbers and check each one against the actual filing or report. If they don't match, stop there. Nothing else in the model is trustworthy until those numbers are real.
2. **Switch to formula view and hunt for hardcodes:** Hit Ctrl + \` to see the formulas behind every cell. Look for numbers that were typed in by hand where a calculation should be instead. These often show up in blue font inside a column that's supposed to be all formulas.
3. **Confirm the statements match up:** Check that the balance sheet balances in every period, and that the cash flow report matches the actual change in cash. If something's off, that's where the model broke.
4. **Test the interest and debt loop:** Make sure interest and debt work themselves out correctly instead of one getting stuck. Check whether the model is set up to solve that loop on its own, or whether it's been switched off to quietly hide an error.
5. **Pressure-test the assumptions:** Look at growth, margins, and the discount rate (the rate used to value future cash today) against what's realistic for this company. AI tends to default to numbers that sound reasonable. Reasonable doesn't always mean right.
6. **Run a sensitivity check:** Change one key number and watch how much the output moves. If a small change in growth barely moves the final result, something isn't connected the way it should be. A quick[sensitivity analysis](https://julius.ai/articles/sensitivity-analysis) also shows you which assumptions actually drive the answer.


**💡 Tip:** The cleaner your inputs going in, the less you'll be fixing on the way out. Most audit pain traces back to messy or wrong source data. **The** model structure usually isn't the real problem.

## Frequently asked questions


### Can Claude be used for financial modeling?


Yes, Claude can be used for financial modeling, and Claude for Excel is **one of the stronger options for reasoning through model logic and auditing formulas** . Corporate Finance Institute built its AI modeling course around it. As with any AI, verify its outputs against the source before you rely on them.


### Which AI model is best for finance?


**Claude** is strongest for reasoning and auditing, **Shortcut** for building models directly in Excel, and **ChatGPT** for working inside the workbook while explaining its logic. No single model wins every job, so match the tool to the work in front of you.


### Is AI accurate enough to build a financial model on its own?


**No, AI isn't accurate enough** to build a financial model on its own yet. It produces a fast first draft, but it can invent numbers, type in fixed values where formulas should be, and struggle with interest-debt loops and deal logic like mergers and buyouts. Treat its output as a starting point, and audit it before anyone makes a decision from it.


### Can AI build a DCF model from scratch?


**Yes, AI can build a DCF model from a prompt or a filing** , including cash flow projections and a final company value. The structure usually holds. The assumptions behind it need your review, since that's where AI tends to default to generic numbers that may not fit your company.


### Do you still need to know finance to use AI for modeling?


**Yes** , you still need modeling knowledge to use AI for financial modeling well. The tools speed up the build, but the judgment still comes from you, and you need enough expertise to spot when the AI is confidently wrong. Used well, it saves time.
